h1: Pacing yourself through a long beer festival day
title: Pacing Yourself at a Beer Festival | Craft Beer School
desc: A practical plan for a six hour beer festival: pour sizes, a running tally, food, water and an order that keeps your palate working.
teaser: Six hours, forty taps and one palate. A plan for still tasting properly at 7 pm.
standfirst: A beer festival rewards patience. Most people taste their best beers in the first hour and remember nothing about the last three. This is a plan for a long day that keeps you sharp, safe and still able to tell a saison from a sour by evening.
sections:
Festivals pour small, which makes it easy to lose count. Say the taster glass is 150 ml and the average beer is 6.5% ABV. Each pour holds about 10 ml of pure alcohol, one UK unit. Ten tasters over an afternoon is ten units, the same as three and a half pints of 5% lager. Twenty tasters is twenty units.

The liver clears roughly one unit an hour. A six hour session that adds two units an hour leaves you well behind by evening. The plan below keeps the number low without cutting the number of beers you taste.
Decide your list before you queue

Look at the tap list the night before or in the first fifteen minutes. Pick eight to twelve beers you really want to try and mark them. Everything else is optional. Without a list you drift from stall to stall and drink whatever has the shortest queue.

Order your list light to heavy. Start with lagers, wheat beers and pale ales. Move to IPAs mid afternoon. Leave imperial stouts, barleywines and anything over 9% for the last hour or two. Our guide to tasting at a festival without losing your palate explains why big hops and roast flatten everything that follows.
Share pours and use the dump bucket

The easiest way to halve your intake is to share. Two friends splitting one taster each get to try twice as many beers for the same alcohol. Agree on this before you arrive.

Use the dump bucket without guilt. Brewers do. If a beer has told you what it has to say in three sips, pour the rest away. A 150 ml taster finished out of politeness is 10 ml of alcohol you did not need. If a stall offers a smaller pour, take it.

Judges at beer competitions work this way. They taste dozens of beers in a day from small samples, often 30 to 60 ml each. They rarely finish one. Their notes stay sharp because the alcohol stays low. You can borrow the habit without the scoresheet.

Eat a proper meal before you arrive, with some protein and fat. Food in the stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches the small intestine, where most of it is absorbed. Our guide to eating before drinking explains the mechanism.

Then eat again every two to three hours. Plain food works best for your palate as well as your stomach. Bread, rice dishes, a plate of chips. A fiery chicken curry at 3 pm will numb your tongue for the next hour of IPAs.

Drink a glass of water with every beer, not every few beers. It slows your pace, rinses your palate and stops thirst from driving you to the next pour. At an outdoor festival in Indian heat you may need a litre or more over the afternoon beyond that, so carry a bottle and refill it.

A water glass also gives your hands something to hold while you talk. That small habit cuts more tasters from a day than willpower does.
Take breaks the brewers would take

Sit down for twenty minutes every couple of hours. Step out of the crowd and the noise. Write a line or two about the beers you liked. Your nose recovers in fresh air faster than it does next to a stall pouring hazy IPA all afternoon.

Keep a running tally. A simple tick in your phone notes for each taster is enough. When the count reaches your limit, switch to water and any alcohol free beer on offer.

Decide how you will get home before you leave the house. Book a cab, agree on a sober driver or take the metro. Do not ride a two wheeler or drive after a festival, however long you have spent drinking water. The legal limit in India is 30 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood, which a few tasters can reach.

Before your next festival, write your list of ten beers in light to heavy order. Then decide which three you will share and book the ride home.
faqs: How many beers can I try at a festival?
Fewer than you think if you finish every pour. Sharing tasters and using the dump bucket lets you try ten or more while keeping your total alcohol modest.
Should I drink water at a beer festival?
Yes. A glass of water with every beer slows your pace, keeps your palate fresh and helps in hot weather.
What order should I taste beers at a festival?
Light to heavy. Lagers and wheat beers first, then pale ales and IPAs, then strong dark beers at the end.
Is it rude to pour beer into the dump bucket?
No. Brewers expect it at festivals. Tasting a few sips and pouring the rest is normal.
